title: The $27,000 Problem: Musasa’s Broken Pump and the Cost of Waiting
subtitle: Water trucks brought relief to Musasa in July. Residents still wanted the pump repaired.
excerpt: In June, a Musasa resident described spending 210,000 Burundian francs a month on water after a pump failure. Emergency deliveries arrived in July. Residents were still asking for the pump to be repaired.

content.text: Sifa spent around 210,000 Burundian francs per month on water bills alone, SOS Médias Burundi reported in June 2026. She lived in the Musasa refugee camp in northern Burundi, with ten people in her household. She spent World Food Programme aid on water and had little money left for food or health care. Local sources told the outlet that replacing the pump's faulty motor would cost about $27,000. For more than six months, more than 9,000 Congolese refugees living in the camp had faced unreliable water supply.

In July, SOS Médias Burundi reported that UNHCR began trucking in water from Gasorwe to fill the camp's water tanks to supply taps. Residents had noticed reduced water bills and were concerned that a lack of fuel could disrupt the process, so they were asking that the pump be repaired and regular power supplied to run it.
What to expect while you wait for repairs

For some residents of Uganda’s Nakivale settlement, getting water meant traveling about eight kilometers to Lake Nakivale; others bought water delivered on bicycles. SOS Médias Burundi reported the prolonged outage in July 2026. According to a medical source cited by the outlet, people were showing symptoms of cholera and typhoid and the hospital had no drinking water. UNHCR staff said there were no funds to buy basic supplies.

Radio Ergo reported in March 2026 on similar water supply disruptions in Hagadera refugee camp, one of the refugee camps in Dadaab, Kenya. Camp officials said at least four boreholes broke last year and were not properly repaired. Deputy Chairman Abukar Sheikh Abdullahi said the camp administration could not afford the repairs. Nimo, a resident interviewed by the media, had food at home but no water for cooking.

content.caption: People collect water at a communal supply point. Editorial stock photograph.

content.text: In November 2025, UNHCR projected that available funding at the end of the year would be approximately $3.9 billion, a 25% decrease from 2024 levels. Early pledges for 2026 totalled about $1.5 billion, or about 18% of projected needs, with more contributions expected. Agencywide data does not show the amount of funding available to repair the Musasa water system.

In May 2025, the World Food Programme warned that starting in June, refugees in Kenya assisted by the program would only receive 28% of full in-kind rations, and that cash assistance would be stopped without additional funds. If a household uses its food allowance to buy water, it has less cash to spend on food. People who cannot buy water have to spend time getting it or wash less often.

Lucy Earle, Kate Crawford and Margarita Garfias Royo discuss government resistance to permanent infrastructure in Zaatari, Jordan, and the issue of trucking water in Forced Migration Review. By mid-2019, some networks had been established, but a survey conducted in 2022 showed that 30% of households reported water shortages, and key informants said that truck deliveries were still necessary during the summer.

content.alt: Families with containers beside a large water tank
content.caption: Families collect water beside a storage tank. Editorial stock photograph.

content.text: The authors were unable to find a breakdown of the costs associated with the Zaatari water system. A budget assessment of the broader Jordanian water, sanitation and hygiene program shows budgets of about $355 million for 2013-2017 and $139 million for 2018-2022, but there is little information on spending. Without reliable records of expenditures in Zaatari, the authors were unable to compare its costs with those of water and sanitation provision in urban areas.

The University of Colorado Boulder explains a system for early detection of failures. The Drought Resilience Impact Platform (DRIP) uses satellite-connected sensors, groundwater and rainfall data, and drought forecasts. Partners include the Millennium Water Alliance and Virridy, as well as local agencies. They use this data to plan maintenance and water service contracts.

A sensor cannot replace the motor, arrange its delivery or pay for a repair. Before adopting a similar system, a settlement would need to decide who receives alerts, who handles repairs and which funds that person can spend without waiting for another emergency appeal.
Water use plan for next year

Launched in Kenya in March 2025, the Shirika Plan aims to integrate refugee services into national and local systems. Speaking at the launch, UNHCR’s Filippo Grandi stressed that local authorities need resources to serve both refugees and host communities. Each site should still decide who can pay for local repairs.

The July deliveries provided residents with water, although they still asked for the pump to be repaired. Future costs will include electricity, wear parts and repairman labor. Water systems need funding to pay these costs and the authority to spend them. In Musasa, families like Sifa's had to pay water bills when the water supply failed.
